Do Snapshot Tests Help in Agent-Driven Development?

An empirical analysis of 311 pull requests in the openhands-cli repository, where 68% of PRs are authored by AI agents.

  2. Finding 1: Snapshots as a Development Forcing Function

§1 Context & Dataset

We mined all 311 merged PRs from the openhands-cli repo (Sep 2025 – May 2026), classified each by type, authorship, and snapshot involvement, then analyzed commit-level history to understand how snapshot tests are actually used.

311Total PRs 68%Agent-authored 46Touch snapshots 11.5→6.5%Critical bug rate

Snapshot tests were adopted in January 2026. Before that, zero PRs touched snapshot files. After adoption, 19–33% of monthly PRs include snapshot changes.

§2 Finding 1: Snapshots as a Development Forcing Function

The strongest signal in the data. After snapshot adoption, 46% of TUI-changing feature PRs now include snapshot updates — up from 0%. This means nearly every visual change must pass through a "did you mean to change how this looks?" gate.

What this means: Snapshot tests create a mandatory visual-diff step in the development workflow. Developers (both human and agent) cannot change the TUI without consciously acknowledging the visual impact and updating baselines.

The green line shows TUI feature PRs including snapshot updates climbing from 0% to 100%. Bug-fix PRs (red) follow at ~35–50% — lower because 35% of all bugs are entirely non-visual (API, config, CLI core — see §7), and even among visual bugs, 76% are on uncovered code paths.

§3 Finding 2: Snapshot Tests Break During Development

This is the finding that most surprised us, and it required commit-level data to see. Of 27 multi-commit snapshot PRs (excluding version bumps), 18 (67%) show a clear pattern: code is written first, then a later commit fixes the snapshot tests.

18 of 27 multi-commit PRs show the "code first, update snapshots later" pattern — evidence that snapshot tests broke during development and had to be fixed before merge.

This is visible in the commit messages themselves:

PR #504 — fix: default collapsibles to collapsed state
[1] fix: default collapsibles to collapsed state
[2] test: update snapshots for collapsed cells default
[3] fix: add retry mechanism for flaky snapshot test
[4] fix: increase retry count for flaky snapshot test
PR #497 — tui: only show agent name prefix for non-default agents
[1] tui: only show agent name prefix for non-default agents
[2] Update richlog_visualizer.py
[3] test: add tests for default agent prefix behavior
[4] Fix CI: update TUI snapshot tests and pyright typing
[5] Merge main and update snapshots
[7] Update snapshot tests after merge from main
PR #490 — tui: remove grey vertical border from Collapsible widgets (refactor, 732 lines)
[1] tui: remove grey vertical border
[2] tui: add color to collapse/expand symbol
[3] tui: remove indentation from Collapsible widgets
[4] fix: use tuple instead of Text and update snapshots
[5] style: indent collapsible content with left padding
[7] fix: update test and snapshots for action/obs default symbol color
[10] Update snapshots after merging from main
What this means: Snapshot tests are functioning as a CI safety net. Developers write code, push it, snapshot tests fail in CI, and they come back to fix the baselines. This is the "regression catch" behavior — it's just happening within a PR rather than between PRs, and it's only visible at the commit level.

§4 Finding 3: Bug Fixes Update Existing Baselines, Not Add New Ones

Of the 12 bug-fix PRs that include snapshot changes, 9 (75%) only modify existing snapshot files — they don't add new tests. This tells us existing snapshot coverage already covered the affected UI states.

9 of 12 bug-fix PRs only modify existing baselines. These aren't adding retroactive test coverage — the tests already existed and their output changed with the fix.

Across all PR types, modified files vastly outnumber added files. Version bumps are entirely modifications (they update the version string visible in every snapshot).

What this means: Snapshot tests are acting as regression baselines. When a bug fix changes the UI, existing snapshots force an intentional visual diff. But this is documentation of the fix, not bug discovery — the bugs themselves were found through other means (user reports, manual testing).

§5 Finding 4: Faster Reviews for Snapshot PRs

Despite being substantially larger (median 850 vs 100 lines changed), TUI PRs with snapshot changes get their first review nearly twice as fast (0.9h vs 1.7h).

Left: first-review time is ~2× faster for snapshot PRs. Right: those same PRs are ~8× larger. SVG diffs lower the barrier to starting a review.

What this means: SVG snapshot diffs give reviewers instant visual understanding of what changed, which is especially valuable for agent-authored code where the reviewer didn't write the code. The visual diff substitutes for manually running the app to verify the UI.

§6 Finding 5: Compounding Value Through Suite Reuse

The 23 snapshot test suites aren't write-once artifacts. The top suites are exercised by 15–23 different PRs each, meaning their regression baselines are continuously validated as the codebase evolves.

HistoryPanelFlow is touched by 23 PRs. Every one of those PRs had to pass (or intentionally update) that visual baseline.

12 of 23 suites have been involved in bug-fix PRs (right bars). HistoryPanelFlow and InitialSetup suites appear in the most bug-fixes — these are the high-churn areas where snapshot regression coverage pays off most.

§7 The Coverage Gap: 85% of Bug-Fixes Ship Uncovered

First, where do bugs actually live? Not all bugs are visual — and snapshot tests can only help with bugs that change rendered output.

The largest category is TUI widgets & screens (38), where 12 involved snapshots (green). But 27 bugs (35%) are entirely non-visual: CLI core, config/state, API/auth. Snapshot tests are structurally irrelevant for these. Even within the visual categories, settings logic (7) and other TUI (6) have zero snapshot involvement.

Critical bugs skew non-visual (44%) — crashes, auth failures, dependency issues. UX regressions are predominantly visual (75%), which is where snapshots have the most theoretical coverage. But even there, only a fraction actually involves snapshots.

The coverage gap within visual bugs

Focusing on bugs where snapshots could help, we need to frame bug-fixes into three categories:

  • No snapshots touched — the bug was in an uncovered area before, and the fix didn't add coverage. A blind spot that remains blind.
  • Modified existing snapshots — the fix changed visual behavior in an area that already had baseline coverage. The change is acknowledged and the new state is locked in.
  • Added new snapshots — genuinely extending coverage to a previously-uncovered area. The correct thing to do.

85% of bug-fix PRs ship without touching snapshots at all. Only 1% added new coverage. The team is overwhelmingly fixing bugs without closing the coverage gap.

Existing snapshots guard behavior during code churn

The commit-level data reveals the most concrete evidence of snapshot value. Across feature, bug-fix, refactor, and test PRs, there were 58 distinct commits where a developer had to go back and fix snapshot tests that broke after their initial code change.

Feature PRs generated the most snapshot-fix commits (24, across 9 PRs). Every one of these is evidence: a feature was being built, it changed something visual that existing snapshots covered, and the developer had to consciously address it. Refactors generated 11 snapshot-fix commits — code restructuring was caught changing visual output.

The key finding: 9 out of 9 multi-commit feature PRs with snapshots had to fix snapshot tests AFTER their initial code. 100%. Every single feature that touched snapshot-covered areas had existing behavior guarded by the test suite. The snapshots didn't prevent the change — they made it visible and forced a conscious decision.

Where bugs actually hit: path-level coverage

The previous version of this analysis defined "covered" too loosely — a bug in textual_app.py was counted as "covered" just because that file appeared in some snapshot PR. But if the bug-fix PR didn't update any snapshots, the specific bug path wasn't covered. The file having coverage elsewhere is irrelevant — it's a false sense of security.

Only 34% of post-adoption TUI bugs (green) hit paths actually guarded by snapshots. 57% (orange) are in files that have some snapshot coverage, but the specific bug path was uncovered — the fix didn't touch snapshots. 9% (red) are in fully uncovered areas. Combining orange + red: 66% of bugs are on uncovered code paths.

Accounting for indirect coverage

Snapshot tests don't just test rendering — they implicitly test the full stack behind what's rendered. A test that renders a conversation after switching implies it exercises conversation persistence. We re-examined all 20 "file covered, path uncovered" bugs by reading every snapshot test file in the repo and asking: would the snapshot output actually change if this bug existed?

The strict criteria for "indirectly covered" (B1):

  1. A snapshot test exercises a flow that runs through this code path
  2. The specific bug would produce visibly different snapshot output
  3. The test's input data (trajectory/mock data) would trigger the bug

After accounting for indirect coverage, 46% of TUI bugs hit covered paths (up from 34%). 4 bugs are indirectly covered (confirmation scrolling, conversation switching, command truncation, autoscrolling). But 16 bugs (46%) are in files with adjacent coverage where no snapshot exercises the specific broken behavior — settings persistence, notifications, event types not in trajectories, race conditions.

The biggest gap: settings persistence. 7 of 16 adjacent-but-uncovered bugs are in settings_screen.py and related modules. The repo has snapshot tests for the first-time setup flow (no saved config) and the critic settings tab, but no test saves settings, closes the modal, and reopens to verify the saved values rendered correctly. A single "save → reload → snapshot" test would indirectly cover model name persistence, condensation defaults, dropdown ordering, and clear behavior — closing 7 bugs' worth of blind spots.

The UX regression rate, honestly normalized

Measuring "% of agent PRs that are UX bugs" is misleading when monthly sample sizes range from 5 to 63. The right normalization: UX bugs per cumulative TUI feature shipped. This controls for codebase growth.

Pre-adoption (grey): the bug-per-feature rate rose from 0 to 0.45 as the codebase grew rapidly. Post-adoption (orange): Jan 2026 started at 0.44 (same level — the adoption month coincided with a huge feature push). Then it drops to 0.10, 0.02, 0.00, 0.07. The settled post-adoption rate (Feb–Apr) is 4–20× lower than the pre-adoption peak.

§8 What Snapshots Don't Do: Reduce the Bug Count

The data does not support the claim that snapshot tests reduce the overall bug rate. The TUI bug-to-feature ratio went from 0.60 to 0.95 after snapshot adoption.

Critical bugs dropped (11.5% → 6.5%) but UX regressions rose (12.6% → 18.5%). The severity shift tracks codebase growth, not snapshot adoption.

Why not? Because 85% of bug-fixes don't involve snapshots. You can't prevent bugs in areas you don't cover. The problem isn't that snapshot tests don't work — it's that only 15% of the codebase's bug surface has them.

§9 Verdict

Snapshot tests are helpful — but the biggest problem is the coverage gap.

Where snapshots exist, they work. The evidence is concrete:

  • 100% of feature PRs in snapshot-covered areas had to fix broken snapshots during development (9/9 multi-commit feature PRs). Existing behavior was guarded.
  • 58 snapshot-fix commits across 20 PRs show developers being forced to acknowledge visual changes — the "code first, fix snapshots later" pattern at the commit level.
  • Reviewers respond 2× faster to snapshot PRs (0.9h vs 1.7h) despite them being 8× larger. SVG diffs provide instant visual understanding.
  • Top test suites are exercised by 15–23 PRs each, compounding their regression value with every change.

But the data is equally clear about the limitation:

  • 85% of bug-fix PRs ship without touching snapshots. The bug was uncovered before the fix, and the fix didn't add coverage. The blind spot remains.
  • Only 1 of 78 bug-fix PRs added new snapshot coverage retroactively.
  • The bug rate didn't decrease — because you can't prevent bugs in areas you don't cover.

The value of snapshot tests is in the development process — making visual changes visible, reviewable, and intentional. This is especially important when an AI agent is writing the code and can't visually inspect its own output. But the team is underinvesting in coverage: bugs are being fixed without extending the safety net to prevent recurrence.

Evidence strength across SDLC phases. Development forcing function has the strongest evidence. Bug prevention has none.

Analysis of 311 PRs from openhands-cli. Data mined via GitHub API; PR types classified with gpt-4o-mini. Graphs generated with matplotlib. Full data and scripts at snapshot-tests-analysis.
